Pelot et al. (2020), vagus nerve morphology of human, pig and rat, on SPARC:60¶

Paper. Pelot, Goldhagen, Cariello, Musselman, Clissold, Ezzell and Grill (2020), "Quantified Morphology of the Cervical and Subdiaphragmatic Vagus Nerves of Human, Pig, and Rat", Front. Neurosci. 14, 601479, doi:10.3389/fnins.2020.601479. The claims file (claims/pelot-2020.yaml) was written from the version of record (Europe PMC, PMC7672126), without the supplement and with Eqs. 1 to 4 lost in the text.

Dataset. SPARC:60, "Quantified morphology of the rat vagus nerve", version 5 (doi:10.26275/lg3c-1kjf, published 2025-02-24), read from the public SPARC bucket at the object versions its manifest gives. Version 5 is the latest and the version the run was given; the paper cites none. Versions 1 to 4 date from 2020; the data check below compares the files the analysis reads in version 5 with version 4 (2020-09-30), the version current when the paper was published.

Sister datasets. The paper's human and pig data are in three other SPARC datasets that list the paper as IsDescribedBy: SPARC:65 (human anti-claudin-1 IHC), SPARC:64 (pig Masson's trichrome) and SPARC:89 (pig anti-fibronectin IF), the paper's Pelot et al. (2020a, f and b). They are used for the claims the claims file marks with_inputs or elsewhere. The paper's supplement cites SPARC:65 version 6 (doi:10.26275/nluu-1ews) and SPARC:89 version 1 (doi:10.26275/8pc2-rhu2), which are pinned; its reference list stops before 2020f, so SPARC:64 is pinned at its latest version, 4 (doi:10.26275/maq2-eii4, 2020-10-01). The human values are recomputed here from the human traces; the pig values come from the per-fascicle output files the paper's code wrote (PigVNMorphology_OutputMetrics.mat, PigIFMorphology.mat), as recomputing the pig traces was out of the time available.

Supplement. The literature values of Supplement 4 (Data_Sheet_2.xlsx), which the claims file's reader did not have, are read from the supplementary files of the version of record in Europe PMC (PMC7672126) and checked against their SHA-256. The supplement's PDF (Data_Sheet_1.pdf) is read there too, for Supplement 6 (the age plots) and the legend of Supplementary Figure 16 (the rat carotid sheath).

Mixed models. The paper fits them in JMP Pro 14.3.0 without giving its settings. They are fitted here by REML with unbounded variance components, JMP's default, and tested with Kenward-Roger F tests computed on the observed REML information (the Hessian of the REML log-likelihood). This choice is an assumption, made because it gives the paper's F and p for all nine effects the paper reports (to within 0.4% for F, and p to the digits printed, with the rat fascicle values the paper's code takes; see "Which test the paper's F and p come from"). Kenward-Roger on the expected information, Satterthwaite, residual and subject-based degrees of freedom and a bounded fit are variants.

Checksums. Every file is checked against the SHA-256 of its version's manifest as it is read; the cell before the summary prints the SHA-256 of each file read.

No random draws. No analysis here draws random numbers, so no seed is needed and nothing is seed sensitive.

**Study Purpose:** To quantify rat vagus nerve morphology

**Data Collection:** Using micrographs of rat vagus nerve cross sections that were stained with Masson’s trichrome, we quantified effective nerve and fascicle diameters, the number of fascicles, and the perineurium thickness at the cervical and subdiaphragmatic levels. These morphological data provide neural anatomical information, as well as foundational knowledge for computational and preclinical studies of vagus nerve stimulation. The dataset contains TIFF files for 9 left cervical and 9 anterior subdiaphragmatic rat vagus nerve samples, providing segmented traces of inner and outer perineurial boundaries, as well as outer nerve boundaries in multifascicular cases.

**Primary Conclusion:** None stated

---
**Curator's Notes**

**Experimental Design:** We segmented Masson’s trichrome micrographs of 9 left cervical and 9 anterior subdiaphragmatic rat vagus nerves using Nikon’s NIS-Elements to identify perineurial and neural boundaries. Using the resulting binary traces, we quantified the effective nerve and fascicle diameters, the number of fascicles, and the perineurium thickness.

**Completeness:** This dataset is part of a larger study "Quantified vagus nerve morphology across species".

**Subjects & Samples:** Adult male (n=5) and female (n=5) Sprague-Dawley rats were used for this study, 65 - 268 days old.

**Primary vs derivative data:** Data in the primary and derivative folders are divided by subject number (listed in subject file), then sample number (listed in sample file). The __primary folder__ contains segmentations of rat Masson's trichrome histology (original histological micrographs are in a prior dataset) shown as TIFF images of the binary traces of the fascicles and nerves (loaded and analyzed by Matlab scripts in the "code" folder). The __derivative folder__ contains a .mat file with the morphology metrics output by the code, as well as xml and jp2 versions of the image files; Neurolucida 360 from MBF Bioscience was used to convert the binary traces into xml file format to overlay with the original Masson’s trichrome nd2 micrographs (in prior dataset) and then to convert the images to jp2 extension.

**Code Availability:** In the "code" folder, Matlab code is used to load the segmented/binary TIFF images, analyze the images, and plot the resulting morphology metrics. **Filepaths in the code are set to work as-is, in-place in the dataset.**
===== files/derivative/README.txt
Image data (.jp2) was derived from primary images (.nd2) in parent dataset (N:dataset:6fa2666c-aa3d-4e27-a405-7848fc061b04). Images were converted with 20:1 compression to .jp2 by MBF Bioscience for web streaming and visualization on the SPARC Data Portal. 

Segmentation data (.xml) was derived from binary mask images of cross sections of rat vagus nerves in primary folder. The process of converting binary masks to MBF XML is detailed on protocols.io (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.bchjit4n) and was performed by MBF Bioscience. Each .xml in the derived sample subfolders correlates to the binary mask images in the primary sample subfolders. 


===== files/code/README.txt
Filepaths in the code are set to work as-is, in-place in the dataset.

Part 1: AnalyzeAllSamples.m
- Load binary TIF images for samples listed in Excel files.
- Use polyarea to calculate cross-sectional area of each inner perineurium trace, outer perineurium trace, and nerve trace.
- Calculate the morphology metrics of interest (effective nerve diameter, effective fascicle diameter, perineurium thickness, ...).
- Save the morphology metrics to .mat files.

Part 2: DataExtraction_v3.m
- Load the morphology metrics into data structures.

Part 3: DataPlotting_v4.m
- DataExtraction_v3.m must be called first to load the data.
- Plot and save the nerve morphology metrics.
     - sub_sam (subject #-sample #; see subjects.xlsx and samples.xlsx)
     - level (C=cervical, A=abdominal i.e. subdiaphragmatic)
     - laterality (L=left [cervical], R=right [cervical], A=anterior [abdominal], P=posterior [abdominal])
     - sex (F=female, M=male)
     - dNerve_um (diameter of circle with same cross-sectional area as nerve trace, in microns)
     - dFasc_um (diameter of circle with same cross-sectional area as fascicle trace, i.e. inner perineurium trace, in microns)
     - NFasc (number of fascicles)
     - thkperi_um (perineurium thickness, half of difference between effective diameter of outer perineurium trace and effective diameter of inner perineurium trace).

The rat samples. The level comes from specimen anatomical location in samples.xlsx. Each sample is measured from its primary traces with the paper's method (vagus.py).

smp = samples.merge(subjects[["subject_id", "age", "body mass"]], on="subject_id", suffixes=("", "_subj"))
smp["sub"] = smp["subject_id"].str[4:].astype(int)
smp["sam"] = smp["sample_id"].str[4:].astype(int)
smp["label"] = "R" + smp["sub"].astype(str) + "-" + smp["sam"].astype(str)
smp["level"] = np.where(smp["specimen anatomical location"].str.contains("cervical"), "cervical", "subdiaphragmatic")
smp["side"] = np.where(smp["specimen anatomical location"].str.startswith("left"), "left",
                       np.where(smp["specimen anatomical location"].str.contains("subdiaphragmatic"), "anterior (by readme)", "?"))
smp["age_days"] = smp["age_subj"].str.replace(" days", "").astype(int)
rat = {}
for _, row in smp.iterrows():
    rat[row["label"]] = v.rat_sample(row["sub"], row["sam"])
smp["n_fasc"] = [rat[l]["n_fasc"] for l in smp["label"]]
smp["um_per_px"] = [rat[l]["um_per_px"] for l in smp["label"]]
smp["image_px"] = [rat[l]["shape"] for l in smp["label"]]
smp["nerve_mask_used"] = [rat[l]["nerve_from_mask"] for l in smp["label"]]
print(smp[["label", "level", "side", "sex", "age_days", "body mass", "Scale Bar Length", "um_per_px", "image_px", "n_fasc", "nerve_mask_used"]].to_string())

Duplicates: no two traces are identical (the SHA-256 of each PeriMask's pixels), and the files the analysis reads are the same S3 objects (same object version and size) in version 4 (2020-09-30) as in version 5.

The measurements against the output files the paper's code wrote. The code folder's RatVNMorphology_OutputMetrics.mat (written 2020-09-05) holds the 18 rat samples as the statistics used them (DataPlotting_v4.m). The derivative folder's file of the same name (written 2020-03-03) is another, older output.

The human and pig data¶

Human: the 18 samples of the paper are those of CadaverVNMorphology_OutputMetrics.mat in SPARC:65's code folder (written 2020-09-05), each measured here from its traces (PeriInnerMask, PeriExtMask, NerveMask), and checked against that file. Pig MT: the 18 samples of PigVNMorphology_OutputMetrics.mat in SPARC:64's code folder (nerve diameter, every fascicle diameter, fascicle count). Pig IF: PigIFMorphology.mat in SPARC:89's code folder (per sample, non-peanut fascicle diameters and perineurium thicknesses, and the tissue proportions), whose sample levels are taken from its per-level lists (pigIF_thkperi_UniqueAges), and SPARC:89's traces for the trace counts.

pif = v.mat("89", "files/code/PigIFMorphology.mat")
def _flat(a):
    out = []
    for x in np.atleast_1d(a):
        if isinstance(x, np.ndarray) and x.dtype == object:
            out.extend(np.atleast_1d(y).astype(float) for y in x)
        else:
            out.append(np.atleast_1d(x).astype(float))
    return out
if_d, if_t = _flat(pif["pigIF_dfasc_notpeanut"]), _flat(pif["pigIF_thkperi"])
if_dall = _flat(pif["pigIF_dfasc"])
if_endo, if_peri = _flat(pif["pigIF_Aendoperc"]), _flat(pif["pigIF_Aperiperc"])
if_nerve = _flat(pif["pigIF_dnerve"])
lvl_lists = [np.concatenate([np.atleast_1d(a).astype(float) for a in pif["pigIF_thkperi_UniqueAges"][k]]) for k in range(2)]
if_level = []
for t in if_t:
    inl = [np.isin(np.round(t, 10), np.round(L, 10)).all() for L in lvl_lists]
    assert sum(inl) == 1
    if_level.append("cervical" if inl[0] else "subdiaphragmatic")
idx = np.atleast_2d(pif["pigIF_sub_sam_indices"])
subs = np.atleast_1d(pif["pigIF_sub_values"])
pigif = pd.DataFrame(dict(level=if_level, n_nonpeanut=[len(d) for d in if_d], n_inner=[len(d) for d in if_dall],
                          d_nerve=[float(x[0]) for x in if_nerve], endo_pct=[float(x[0]) for x in if_endo],
                          peri_pct=[float(x[0]) for x in if_peri]))
print("PigIFMorphology.mat, per sample in file order (subjects", list(subs), "):")
print(pigif.round(2).to_string())
print("non-peanut fascicles: %d (cervical %d, subdiaphragmatic %d); file's own fit has dfe = %d, R2 = %.4f" %
      (pigif.n_nonpeanut.sum(), pigif[pigif.level == "cervical"].n_nonpeanut.sum(),
       pigif[pigif.level == "subdiaphragmatic"].n_nonpeanut.sum(), pif["pigIF_thkperi_gof"]["dfe"], pif["pigIF_thkperi_gof"]["rsquare"]))
pigif_traces = {}
for p in sorted(v.files("89")):
    if p.endswith("PeriInMask.tif"):
        sub, sam = p.split("/")[2][4:], p.split("/")[3][4:]
        pigif_traces[f"P{sub}-{sam}"] = v.pig_if_counts(int(sub), int(sam))
psamp89 = v.excel("89", "files/samples.xlsx")
loc89 = {f"P{s[4:]}-{m[4:]}": l for s, m, l in zip(psamp89["subject_id"], psamp89["sample_id"], psamp89["specimen anatomical location"])}
pit = pd.DataFrame(pigif_traces).T
pit["level"] = ["cervical" if "cervical" in loc89[k] else "subdiaphragmatic" for k in pit.index]
print(pit.to_string())

Tables used by the claims¶

One row per sample for nerve-level measures and one per fascicle for fascicle diameters. Rat statistics use one fascicle per sample (Methods, "Imaging and Image Analysis", paragraph 2: "for all statistics, we only used the largest fascicle in each rat sample, using the outer perineurial boundary as the nerve boundary"). The largest fascicle is taken here by endoneurial area. DataPlotting_v4.m takes the largest outer perineurium for the nerve, but for the fascicle diameter the first inner trace in its order (fasc_ind == 1), which in R22-1 and R23-1 is not the largest fascicle; the code's values are shown as a variant wherever they differ.

def msd(x):
    return "%.4g +/- %.3g (n = %d)" % (np.mean(x), np.std(x, ddof=1), len(x))

def by(sp, lv, col="d_nerve", df=None):
    df = S if df is None else df
    return df[(df.species == sp) & (df.level == lv)][col].values

The mixed model tests¶

The mixed models are fitted by REML with unbounded variance components (v.reml_unbounded), JMP's default, and each effect is tested with the Kenward-Roger F test (v.kr_setup, v.kr_test) computed on the observed REML information (F_kr_obs, ddf_kr_obs, p_kr_obs); Tukey's HSD uses the adjusted covariance and degrees of freedom of each difference from the same test. The choice is an assumption, made because it gives the paper's F and p (see "Which test the paper's F and p come from", after fascicle-diameter-anova). Kenward-Roger on the expected information, as Kenward and Roger (1997) define it (F_kr, ddf_kr, p_kr), and Wald F tests with Satterthwaite, residual and subject-based degrees of freedom are shown as variants. The check below runs the Kenward-Roger code on a balanced split-plot design, where it must give the exact F tests.

In [11]:
# Kenward-Roger check on a balanced split-plot design without random draws: 3 species x 6
# subjects, each subject at both levels, one value per cell. There the Kenward-Roger tests are
# the exact split-plot F tests: species against the between-subject error, level and the
# interaction against the within-subject error, each with 15 degrees of freedom.
k_ = np.arange(36)
toy = pd.DataFrame(dict(species=np.repeat(["a", "b", "c"], 12), subject=np.repeat(np.arange(18), 2), level=np.tile(["x", "y"], 18)))
toy["y"] = np.sin(1.7 * k_) + 0.8 * np.cos(2.3 * toy.subject) + 0.4 * (toy.level == "x") + 0.3 * (toy.species == "b")
tab_toy, _, _ = v.reml_unbounded(toy, "y", "subject")
sm_ = toy.groupby("subject").agg(species=("species", "first"), m=("y", "mean"))
d_ = toy.pivot(index="subject", columns="level", values="y")
d_ = (d_["x"] - d_["y"]).to_frame("d").join(sm_.species)
mse_ = sum(((g.d - g.d.mean()) ** 2).sum() for _, g in d_.groupby("species")) / 15
exact = [stats.f_oneway(*[g.m for _, g in sm_.groupby("species")]).statistic, d_.d.mean() ** 2 / (mse_ / 18),
         stats.f_oneway(*[g.d for _, g in d_.groupby("species")]).statistic]
print(tab_toy[["term", "df", "F_kr_obs", "ddf_kr_obs", "F_kr", "ddf_kr", "p_kr", "df_satt"]].assign(F_exact=exact, ddf_exact=15).round(4).to_string())

Result: reproduced. The dataset holds nine cervical and nine subdiaphragmatic rat samples, 4F and 5M at each level, from 10 Sprague-Dawley rats (5M, 5F) aged 75 to 268 days with body mass 381.1 +/- 118.4 g, as the Methods give. The cervical samples are all left; the subdiaphragmatic samples are described as "subdiaphragmatic vagus nerve" without the side, which the readme gives as anterior. R18 has only a cervical sample (R18-1) and R26 only a subdiaphragmatic one. No right cervical or posterior samples are deposited, and the code's lists for them are empty. The readme says 65 to 268 days; subjects.xlsx gives 75.

rat-nerve-diameter¶

Rat vagus nerves have effective diameters of 0.260 +/- 0.025 mm at the cervical level and 0.135 +/- 0.015 mm at the subdiaphragmatic level.

rat-multifascicular-proportions¶

Counting all segmented fascicles and the surrounding tissue, the epineurium, perineurium and endoneurium proportions are 58.0, 3.8 and 38.2% for R16-1, 55.1, 4.2 and 40.7% for R23-1, and 63.4, 3.6 and 33.0% for R22-1.

In [15]:
exp = {"R16-1": (58.0, 3.8, 38.2), "R23-1": (55.1, 4.2, 40.7), "R22-1": (63.4, 3.6, 33.0)}
ok = 0
for lab, e in exp.items():
    r = rat[lab]
    endo = 100 * r["endo_area"] / r["nerve_area"]
    peri = 100 * r["peri_area"] / r["nerve_area"]
    epi = 100 - endo - peri
    got = (epi, peri, endo)
    within = [abs(g - x) <= 0.1 * x + 1e-9 for g, x in zip(got, e)]
    ok += sum(within)
    print(lab, "epineurium %.1f, perineurium %.2f, endoneurium %.1f %% | expected %s | within 10%%: %s" % (epi, peri, endo, e, within))
print("values within 10%%: %d of 9" % ok)

The paper's code takes the first inner trace in its order, which is not the largest fascicle in R22-1 (39.35 against 105.76 um) and R23-1 (142.15 against 147.47 um); with its values the subdiaphragmatic mean is 0.1211 mm (SD 0.0323), the paper's numbers. nerve-diameter-anova¶

Effective nerve diameter differs across species and across nerve levels, with no detected interaction of species and level.

The 54 samples: rat from this dataset (largest fascicle's outer perineurium), human from SPARC:65's traces, pig MT from SPARC:64's output file. Subjects are coded per species.

The Methods fit the models in JMP Pro 14.3.0, whose REML default allows negative variance components ("Unbounded Variance Components"), and do not give its tests. The main fit here is REML with unbounded variance components (vagus.reml_unbounded), tested by Kenward-Roger F on the observed information (F_kr_obs, ddf_kr_obs, p_kr_obs); Tukey tests use the covariance and degrees of freedom of each difference from the same test. Kenward-Roger on the expected information (F_kr, ddf_kr, p_kr), the Wald F with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (p_satt), with the residual degrees of freedom and with subjects minus fixed parameters are variants, and so is the statsmodels REML fit, whose subject variance cannot go below zero.

In [17]:
tab_nd, vc_nd, fit_nd = v.reml_unbounded(S, "d_nerve_mm", "subject")
print("unbounded REML: variance components", {k: round(x, 5) for k, x in vc_nd.items()}, "| converged:", fit_nd["converged"])
print(tab_nd.round(5).to_string())

print("variant, statsmodels REML (bounded): subject variance %.5f" % res_nd.cov_re.iloc[0, 0])
print(tab_nd_b.round(5).to_string())

Result: reproduced (resting on an assumption). With unbounded variance components (the subject variance is estimated at -0.052, against a residual 0.127), the Kenward-Roger tests on the observed information give species F = 577.0 (p < 0.0001), level F = 11.01 (p = 0.0030) and interaction F = 2.4455 (p = 0.1085), against the paper's 577.1, 11.01 (p = 0.0030) and 2.445 (p = 0.1085): species and level are significant and the interaction is not. Kenward-Roger on the expected information gives level p = 0.0023 and interaction p = 0.103, Satterthwaite 0.0029 and 0.108. With the subject variance held at zero or above (statsmodels), the interaction is significant (F = 3.71, p = 0.024), which would make the claim only partially reproduced; the outcome rests on JMP's default of unbounded variance components, which reproduces the paper's F values.

human-pig-nerve-diameter-similar¶

Human and pig vagus nerves have similar effective diameters, 1.9 +/- 0.5 against 2.2 +/- 0.2 mm cervically and 1.7 +/- 0.3 against 1.6 +/- 0.2 mm subdiaphragmatically, with no significant difference by Tukey's test.

In [18]:
for sp in ["human", "pig"]:
    for lv in ["cervical", "subdiaphragmatic"]:
        print(sp, lv, msd(by(sp, lv, "d_nerve_mm")), "mm")
fit_nd_t = dict(fit_nd, use_kr="obs")
tk_sp, means_sp = v.tukey(fit_nd_t, S, [("human", "pig"), ("rat", "human"), ("rat", "pig")], "a")
print("species least squares means (mm):", {k: round(x, 4) for k, x in means_sp.items()})
print(tk_sp.round(5).to_string())

tk_cell, means_cell = v.tukey(fit_nd_t, S, cells, "cell")

tk_sp["p_satt"] = v.tukey(dict(fit_nd, satt=True), S, [("human", "pig"), ("rat", "human"), ("rat", "pig")], "a")[0]["p_tukey"]
tk_sp["p_subject_df"] = v.tukey(dict(fit_nd, dfres=fit_nd["dfsub"]), S, [("human", "pig"), ("rat", "human"), ("rat", "pig")], "a")[0]["p_tukey"]
print(tk_sp.round(5).to_string())

Tukey's test of the species means gives human against pig p = 0.179 (paper 0.1830); with Kenward-Roger on the expected information 0.159, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom 0.157, with subject-based ones 0.143; per level 0.144 and 0.989; with the bounded fit 0.343. Result: reproduced. Rat against human and rat against pig both have Tukey p < 0.0001 (7.9e-14 and 3.1e-12; Kenward-Roger on the expected information 2.1e-15 and a value printed as 0, Satterthwaite 4.3e-14 and 2.6e-12; values this small are at the precision of the studentized range integral), with rat smaller, and the ratios of the rat mean to the human and pig means are 0.134 and 0.117 cervically and 0.081 and 0.082 subdiaphragmatically, all within 0.05 to 0.2. Per level, all four contrasts have p < 0.0001.

nerve-cervical-larger¶

Cervical vagus nerves are larger than subdiaphragmatic nerves, a trend clearest in pigs and rats.

Result: reproduced (resting on an assumption). The level effect has Kenward-Roger p = 0.0030 (on the expected information 0.0023, Satterthwaite 0.0029), and the cervical least squares mean (1.425 mm) exceeds the subdiaphragmatic (1.131 mm). The relative difference of means is 0.127 in humans, 0.254 in pigs and 0.475 in rats, so larger for pigs and rats than for humans, the claims file's reading of "clearest". The rat part alone holds (0.258 against 0.135 mm).

fascicle-number-human-pig¶

Pig vagus nerves have almost ten times more fascicles than human nerves (47 +/- 10 and 38 +/- 7 against 6.7 +/- 4.5 and 4.9 +/- 4.0 at the cervical and subdiaphragmatic levels), the number differs by species and level with no detected interaction, and there are more fascicles cervically.

fascicle-diameter-anova¶

Effective fascicle diameter differs across species and nerve levels, with a significant species by level interaction.

log10 of each fascicle's effective diameter: every inner perineurium trace of the human (104) and pig MT (766) samples, and the largest fascicle of each rat sample (18).

Result: reproduced. On log10 fascicle diameter, the Kenward-Roger tests give species F = 9.59 (p = 0.0011), level F = 46.5 (p < 0.0001) and interaction F = 4.93 (p = 0.015), all below 0.05 (paper 8.989, p = 0.0015; 51.88; 5.273, p = 0.0121). With the rat fascicles as the paper's code takes them, species F = 8.989 (p = 0.0015), level F = 51.88 and interaction F = 5.273 (p = 0.0121), the paper's values. Kenward-Roger on the expected information, the Satterthwaite and the bounded variants also give all three p below 0.05.

Which test the paper's F and p come from¶

The paper gives F and p for nine effects (three models). Each (F, p) pair fixes the denominator degrees of freedom the paper used. Below, those degrees of freedom are solved for and set beside the Wald F with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, the Kenward-Roger test on the expected REML information (Kenward and Roger, 1997) and the Kenward-Roger test on the observed information (the Hessian of the REML log-likelihood, the information the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom use), for the fascicle diameter model with both rat rules.

In [23]:
from scipy import optimize
paper_fp = {"nerve diameter": (tab_nd, [(577.1, None), (11.01, 0.0030), (2.445, 0.1085)]),
            "fascicle number": (tab_nf, [(213.8, None), (5.486, 0.0300), (2.481, 0.1322)]),
            "fascicle diameter, largest fascicle": (tab_fd, [(8.989, 0.0015), (51.88, None), (5.273, 0.0121)]),
            "fascicle diameter, code's rat values": (tab_fdc, [(8.989, 0.0015), (51.88, None), (5.273, 0.0121)])}
rows_fp = []
for model, (tab_, fp) in paper_fp.items():
    for (_, r_), (F_p, p_p) in zip(tab_.iterrows(), fp):
        ddf_p = optimize.brentq(lambda m: stats.f.sf(F_p, r_.df, m) - p_p, 1.01, 1e4) if p_p else np.nan
        rows_fp.append(dict(model=model, term=r_.term, F_paper=F_p, p_paper=p_p, ddf_paper=ddf_p, F_wald=r_.F, ddf_satt=r_.df_satt,
                            p_satt=r_.p_satt, F_kr_exp=r_.F_kr, ddf_kr_exp=r_.ddf_kr, p_kr_exp=r_.p_kr,
                            F_kr_obs=r_.F_kr_obs, ddf_kr_obs=r_.ddf_kr_obs, p_kr_obs=r_.p_kr_obs))
FP = pd.DataFrame(rows_fp)
pd.set_option("display.width", 250)
print(FP.round(4).to_string())
for col in ["F_wald", "F_kr_exp", "F_kr_obs"]:
    m_ = FP.model != "fascicle diameter, largest fascicle"
    print("%-9s largest relative difference from the paper's F (rat values as the code takes them): %.2f%%"
          % (col, 100 * (FP[m_][col] / FP[m_].F_paper - 1).abs().max()))

The Kenward-Roger test on the observed information gives the paper's F to within 0.4% and its p to the digits printed for all nine effects, with the rat fascicle values the paper's code takes for fascicle diameter, and its denominator degrees of freedom are within 1 of those the paper's (F, p) pairs imply (23.0 and 23.5, 19.4 and 18.5, 21.1 and 25.6 against 23.3 and 23.4, 19.3 and 19.3, 21.2 and 25.4). Kenward-Roger on the expected information gives F up to 5.1% off and degrees of freedom up to twice the paper's, the Wald F up to 9.8% off. The observed-information test is therefore taken as the main test for every mixed model claim, still as an assumption (JMP's settings are not given). With the largest fascicle in place of the code's rat values, the fascicle diameter F values are 9.59, 46.5 and 4.93 against the paper's 8.989, 51.88 and 5.273, which shows again that the paper's statistics used the code's rat values.

cervical-fascicle-diameter-species¶

At the cervical level human fascicles (0.355 +/- 0.226 mm) are larger than pig fascicles (0.155 +/- 0.058 mm), while rat fascicles are comparable to both.

Result: reproduced. Human 0.1635 +/- 0.146 mm and pig 0.1101 +/- 0.0438 mm, within the paper's values; no subdiaphragmatic pair differs (human against pig p = 0.300, human against rat 0.996, pig against rat 0.884; paper 0.3049, 0.8960, 0.9947). The log10 differences are 0.146, 0.049 and -0.097, the largest human against pig, as the paper's "trended larger". With the code's rat values the three pairs give 0.306, 0.899 and 0.995, the paper's values.

fascicles-larger-cervical¶

All three species have larger fascicles at the cervical than at the subdiaphragmatic level.

Result: partially reproduced (resting on an assumption). Cervical fascicles are larger in all three species. With Kenward-Roger on the observed information, the test that gives the paper's F and p for the nine effects it reports, human p = 0.00002, pig p = 0.055 and rat p = 0.045 (paper < 0.0001, 0.0009, 0.0234): two of three species have p < 0.05, so partially reproduced. With the code's rat values, which give the paper's F values for this model, human 0.00003, pig 0.060 and rat 0.0093, again two of three. Rounds 1 and 2 verified reproduced, which rested on Kenward-Roger on the expected information (pig p = 0.012, rat 0.044; code's rat values pig 0.013, rat 0.0089), a test the paper's degrees of freedom do not support (see "Which test the paper's F and p come from"). The change to partially reproduced was proposed after round 2 and agreed in round 3. Of the ten combinations of test and rat values printed, six give three species and four give two: Kenward-Roger on the observed information with either rat rule (pig 0.055, 0.060), Satterthwaite with the code's rat values (pig 0.053), and subjects minus parameters with the largest fascicle (rat 0.068), so the outcome depends on the test. The pig contrast has 3.74 degrees of freedom on the observed information and 7.55 on the expected information, the difference lying mostly in the sample variance term (138257 against 243007). No variant gives the paper's pig p of 0.0009: with this contrast's t (4.77), that p needs 24.6 degrees of freedom, and the observed-information test, which gives the paper's other Tukey p values closely, does not give its within-species level contrasts. The rat-only mixed model gives p = 1.7e-07 (largest fascicle) and 0.00033 (code's values), and a paired t test on the 8 rats with both levels p = 8.0e-07.

rat-diameter-like-fascicle¶

The monofascicular rat nerves have diameters close to that of a single human or pig fascicle.

human-pig-tissue-proportions¶

Endoneurium is a larger share of the human nerve cervically (32 +/- 7.9%) than subdiaphragmatically (8.8 +/- 5.3%), while in pigs it is more even across levels (27 +/- 5.3% and 20 +/- 4.0%, MT); perineurium follows the same trends (human 8.9 +/- 2.5% and 3.4 +/- 1.6%, pig 5.1 +/- 1.8% and 4.0 +/- 0.5%).

Human from the traces (endoneurium within inner traces, perineurium between outer and inner traces, over the nerve trace); pig MT endoneurium from the per-fascicle diameters of SPARC:64 (the sum of the fascicles' circle areas over the nerve's circle area, the same areas as the traces' since each diameter is that of the trace's area); pig perineurium from SPARC:89's per-sample IF proportions.

In rats the ratio of mean subdiaphragmatic to mean cervical endoneurial area is 0.32 and the ratio of mean nerve diameters is 0.68.

human-variability¶

Nerve and fascicle diameters are more consistent across samples in pigs (and rats) than in humans.

literature-comparison-human-pig and rat-literature-comparison¶

Human cervical fascicle numbers and endoneurial areas match prior reports while the nerve areas and diameters are generally smaller; human subdiaphragmatic sizes match prior reports; pig fascicle numbers match literature, with slightly smaller mean diameters.

Rat cervical nerve diameters and areas agree with published data, while the rat subdiaphragmatic nerves are slightly larger than prior data.

The literature values are those of Supplement 4 ("Summary statistics and literature review", Data_Sheet_2.xlsx), which the claims file's reader did not have; it is read from the supplementary files of the version of record in Europe PMC (PMC7672126). Its summary columns for this paper's own data are checked against the values measured here. As the criterion says, each literature mean is judged against this paper's mean +/- SD (Figure 7). Every published row is used, left and right: the Results say the comparison includes "data published for both left/right and anterior/posterior VNs", and Figure 7 plots them. The rows of Supplement 4 with no reference, side or n continue the study above them; their notes say they are that study's mean converted between diameter and area (derived). Left-side rows only (this paper's samples are left cervical) and, for the rat, the rows without the converted values are variants.

In [32]:
LIT = v.supplement4()
print("Supplement 4 rows:", len(LIT), "| sections:", list(LIT.section.unique()))
sec = {"area": "Total nerve cross-sectional area (mm^2)", "diam": "Effective nerve diameter (mm)",
       "nfasc": "Number of fascicles (unitless)", "endo": "Endoneurial cross-sectional area (mm^2)"}
lvmap = {"Cervical": "cervical", "Abdominal": "subdiaphragmatic"}
ours = {"area": lambda sp, lv: by(sp, lv, "nerve_area") / 1e6, "diam": lambda sp, lv: by(sp, lv, "d_nerve_mm"),
        "nfasc": lambda sp, lv: by(sp, lv, "n_fasc").astype(float), "endo": lambda sp, lv: by(sp, lv, "endo_area") / 1e6}
chk = []
for key, title in sec.items():
    for (sp, lv), g in LIT[LIT.section == title].groupby(["species", "level"]):
        if sp not in ("Human", "Pig", "Rat"):
            continue
        x = ours[key](sp.lower(), lvmap[lv])
        chk.append(dict(measure=key, species=sp, level=lv, supplement_mean=g.ours_mean.iloc[0], here_mean=x.mean(),
                        supplement_sd=g.ours_sd.iloc[0], here_sd=np.std(x, ddof=1)))
print(pd.DataFrame(chk).round(4).to_string())

def lit_table(key, sp, lv):
    g = LIT[(LIT.section == sec[key]) & (LIT.species == sp) & (LIT.level == lv) & LIT.lit_mean.notna()].copy()
    x = ours[key](sp.lower(), lvmap[lv])
    m, sd = x.mean(), np.std(x, ddof=1)
    g["here_mean"], g["here_sd"], g["here_min"], g["here_max"] = m, sd, x.min(), x.max()
    g["within_mean_sd"] = (g.lit_mean >= m - sd) & (g.lit_mean <= m + sd)
    g["here_below"] = m < g.lit_mean
    lo, hi = g.lit_mean - g.lit_var, g.lit_mean + g.lit_var
    g["ranges_overlap"] = np.where(g.lit_var.notna(), (x.min() <= hi) & (x.max() >= lo), np.nan)
    return g[["reference", "laterality", "sex", "n", "lit_mean", "lit_var", "var_kind", "here_mean", "here_sd", "here_min",
              "here_max", "within_mean_sd", "here_below", "ranges_overlap", "derived", "notes"]]

re_ = LIT[(LIT.section == sec["endo"]) & (LIT.species == "Rat")][["level", "ours_mean", "ours_min", "ours_max"]].drop_duplicates()
print("Supplement 4, rat endoneurial area (mm2):"); print(re_.round(4).to_string())

    by("rat", "subdiaphragmatic", "endo_area_all").mean() / 1e6, by("rat", "subdiaphragmatic", "endo_area_all").max() / 1e6,
    by("rat", "subdiaphragmatic", "endo_area_all").mean() / by("rat", "cervical", "endo_area").mean()))

Supplement 4's summaries of this paper's data equal the values measured here, with one exception: its rat subdiaphragmatic endoneurial area is the area of all segmented fascicles (mean 0.0155, maximum 0.0329 mm2, as here), although its note says the rat data are for the largest fascicle (0.0132 mm2 here). Over all fascicles the ratio to the cervical area is 0.317, the Discussion's 0.32.

parts = {}
for name, key, sp, lv in [("human cervical fascicles", "nfasc", "Human", "Cervical"), ("human cervical endoneurial area", "endo", "Human", "Cervical"),
                          ("human cervical nerve area", "area", "Human", "Cervical"), ("human cervical nerve diameter", "diam", "Human", "Cervical"),
                          ("human subdiaphragmatic nerve area", "area", "Human", "Abdominal"), ("human subdiaphragmatic nerve diameter", "diam", "Human", "Abdominal"),
                          ("human subdiaphragmatic fascicles", "nfasc", "Human", "Abdominal"),
                          ("pig cervical fascicles", "nfasc", "Pig", "Cervical"), ("pig subdiaphragmatic fascicles", "nfasc", "Pig", "Abdominal"),
                          ("pig cervical nerve diameter", "diam", "Pig", "Cervical"), ("pig subdiaphragmatic nerve diameter", "diam", "Pig", "Abdominal")]:
    t = lit_table(key, sp, lv)
    parts[name] = t
    print("=====", name)
    print(t.drop(columns="notes").round(4).to_string())
ant = lambda t: t[t.laterality.astype(str).str.startswith("Ant")]

def human_cervical_verdict(sel):
    return {
        "human cervical fascicles comparable": bool(sel(parts["human cervical fascicles"]).within_mean_sd.all()),
        "human cervical endoneurial areas comparable": bool(sel(parts["human cervical endoneurial area"]).within_mean_sd.all()),
        "human cervical nerve areas smaller": bool(sel(parts["human cervical nerve area"]).here_below.all()),
        "human cervical nerve diameters smaller": bool(sel(parts["human cervical nerve diameter"]).here_below.all()),
        "human cervical below 3.0 mm": bool(by("human", "cervical", "d_nerve_mm").mean() < 3.0),
        "human cervical ranges overlap (where a spread is given)": bool(pd.concat([sel(parts["human cervical nerve area"]),
            sel(parts["human cervical nerve diameter"])]).ranges_overlap.dropna().astype(bool).all()),
    }

verdict = dict(human_cervical_verdict(lambda t: t))
verdict.update({
    "human subdiaphragmatic anterior areas compare well": bool(ant(parts["human subdiaphragmatic nerve area"]).within_mean_sd.all()),
    "human subdiaphragmatic anterior diameters compare well": bool(ant(parts["human subdiaphragmatic nerve diameter"]).within_mean_sd.all()),
    "pig fascicles consistent": bool(parts["pig cervical fascicles"].within_mean_sd.all() and parts["pig subdiaphragmatic fascicles"].within_mean_sd.all()),
    "pig mean diameters smaller": bool(parts["pig cervical nerve diameter"].here_below.all() and parts["pig subdiaphragmatic nerve diameter"].here_below.all()),
})
print("main reading, every published row of Supplement 4 (left and right, as the paper compares them):")
for k, x in verdict.items():
    print("  %-62s %s" % (k, x))
print("parts holding: %d of %d" % (sum(verdict.values()), len(verdict)))
left = human_cervical_verdict(lambda t: t[t.laterality.astype(str) == "L"])
print("variant, human cervical parts against left-side rows only (this paper's samples are left cervical):")
for k, x in left.items():
    print("  %-62s %s" % (k, x))
print("human cervical parts holding: all rows %d of 6, left rows only %d of 6" % (sum(list(verdict.values())[:6]), sum(left.values())))
print("not in the claim's statement (Results, paragraph 8): fewer human subdiaphragmatic fascicles than the posterior study:",
      bool(parts["human subdiaphragmatic fascicles"].here_below.all()))

Result: partially reproduced (resting on an assumption). 8 of the 10 parts of the claim hold. The human cervical fascicle numbers (6.67 +/- 4.5) contain all seven published means (5.0 to 9.14); the human cervical nerve area (3.05 mm2) and diameter (1.92 mm) are below every published mean (3.20 to 8.45 mm2, 2.02 to 3.28 mm), and below 3.0 mm; the human anterior subdiaphragmatic area and diameter contain the anterior published means; the pig fascicle numbers contain the published 46 and 43; the pig diameters (2.20 and 1.64 mm) are below the published 2.93 and 2.09 mm. Two parts fail: the human cervical endoneurial area, 0.922 +/- 0.337 mm2, does not contain Seki et al.'s 1.32 (left) and 1.84 mm2 (right), though it contains Verlinden et al.'s 0.75 and 1.09; and the sample range of human cervical nerve area (0.83 to 5.09 mm2) does not reach Verlinden et al.'s right-side spread (6.0 to 10.9 mm2). Against left-side rows only, 5 of the 6 human cervical parts hold: the ranges overlap, and the endoneurial area still fails on Seki et al.'s left 1.32 mm2. The outcome is the same under both readings. The fewer subdiaphragmatic fascicles than the posterior study (4.89 against 16) holds but is not part of the claim's statement and is not counted. The judgement rules are the claims file's reading of Figure 7.

rparts = {}
for name, key, lv in [("rat cervical nerve diameter", "diam", "Cervical"), ("rat cervical nerve area", "area", "Cervical"),
                      ("rat subdiaphragmatic nerve diameter", "diam", "Abdominal"), ("rat subdiaphragmatic nerve area", "area", "Abdominal")]:
    t = lit_table(key, "Rat", lv)
    rparts[name] = t
    print("=====", name)
    print(t.drop(columns="notes").round(4).to_string())
print("Supplement 4's notes on the rat cervical rows:")
for name in ["rat cervical nerve diameter", "rat cervical nerve area"]:
    for _, r in rparts[name].iterrows():
        print("  %s | %s %s | %.4f | derived %s | %s" % (name, r.reference, r.laterality, r.lit_mean, r.derived, r.notes))

def rat_verdict(sel):
    return {"cervical diameters within mean +/- SD": bool(sel(rparts["rat cervical nerve diameter"]).within_mean_sd.all()),
            "cervical areas within mean +/- SD": bool(sel(rparts["rat cervical nerve area"]).within_mean_sd.all()),
            "subdiaphragmatic diameter above every published mean": bool(rparts["rat subdiaphragmatic nerve diameter"].here_below.eq(False).all()),
            "subdiaphragmatic area above every published mean": bool(rparts["rat subdiaphragmatic nerve area"].here_below.eq(False).all())}

for label, sel in [("main reading, every published row", lambda t: t),
                   ("variant, without the rows Supplement 4 converted between diameter and area", lambda t: t[~t.derived]),
                   ("variant, left-side rows only", lambda t: t[t.laterality.astype(str) == "L"])]:
    rv = rat_verdict(sel)
    print(label + ":", rv)
for name in ["rat cervical nerve diameter", "rat cervical nerve area"]:
    t = rparts[name]
    print("%s: published means %d of %d within mean +/- SD; within the sample range: %d of %d" % (
        name, t.within_mean_sd.sum(), len(t), ((t.lit_mean >= t.here_min) & (t.lit_mean <= t.here_max)).sum(), len(t)))

  rat cervical nerve diameter | Licursi de Alcântara et al. 2008 R | 0.2991 | derived False | Calculated mean(d_nerve) from mean(A_nerve); diameters reported in the paper are the smallest diameter <fill in values>, not effective diameter.
  rat cervical nerve area | Fazan and Lachat 1997 R | 0.0635 | derived False | Used oldest control group (185 days after inoculation). Units of fasicular area in Table 1 of paper incorrectly labeled as mm2; should be *10^-3 mm2. Methods mention samples from proximal & distal cVN, but those sample groups are not mentioned in the results.
  rat cervical nerve area | Fazan and Lachat 1997 R | 0.0400 | derived True | Calculated mean(A_nerve) from mean(d_nerve)
  rat cervical nerve area | Licursi de Alcântara et al. 2008 L | 0.0620 | derived False | Average values from male/female & rostral/caudal cervical vagus nerve samples. Converted SEM from each average value to SD for all 20 samples.
  rat cervical nerve area | Licursi de Alcântara et al. 2008 R | 0.0703 | derived False | Average values from male/female & rostral/caudal cervical vagus nerve samples. Converted SEM from each average value to SD for all 20 samples.
main reading, every published row: {'cervical diameters within mean +/- SD': False, 'cervical areas within mean +/- SD': False, 'subdiaphragmatic diameter above every published mean': True, 'subdiaphragmatic area above every published mean': True}
variant, without the rows Supplement 4 converted between diameter and area: {'cervical diameters within mean +/- SD': False, 'cervical areas within mean +/- SD': False, 'subdiaphragmatic diameter above every published mean': True, 'subdiaphragmatic area above every published mean': True}
variant, left-side rows only: {'cervical diameters within mean +/- SD': True, 'cervical areas within mean +/- SD': True, 'subdiaphragmatic diameter above every published mean': True, 'subdiaphragmatic area above every published mean': True}
rat cervical nerve diameter: published means 1 of 4 within mean +/- SD; within the sample range: 3 of 4
rat cervical nerve area: published means 1 of 4 within mean +/- SD; within the sample range: 3 of 4

Result: partially reproduced (resting on an assumption). The rat subdiaphragmatic nerves are larger than every published value (diameter 0.135 mm against 0.086 to 0.109 mm, area 0.0145 against 0.0058 to 0.0093 mm2). The cervical part fails under the claims file's rule with every published row: one of four published diameter means (0.281 mm, Licursi de Alcantara et al., left) and one of four area means (0.0620 mm2, the same study) lie within the rat mean +/- SD (0.258 +/- 0.025 mm, 0.0526 +/- 0.0102 mm2). Two of the four rows are Fazan and Lachat's right-side nerves converted by Supplement 4 between diameter and area (0.2843 mm, 0.0400 mm2); without them the cervical part still fails (Fazan and Lachat's 0.2257 mm and 0.0635 mm2 and Licursi de Alcantara et al.'s right 0.2991 mm and 0.0703 mm2 lie outside). Against left-side rows only, which hold one study, the cervical part holds and the claim would be reproduced. The readings give different outcomes; the main one uses every row, as the paper compares with left and right nerves and Figure 7 plots them, so the outcome rests on that reading. Three of the four published means lie within the range of the nine samples.

Perineurium thickness against fascicle diameter¶

Non-peanut fascicles only (Figure 9 legend). Human from SPARC:65's traces, pig from SPARC:89's PigIFMorphology.mat, rat from this dataset's traces. Fits by linear least squares (Methods); DataPlotting_v4.m fits poly1 (thickness = p1 d + p2) to every rat fascicle with a thickness, at both levels pooled, and the pig file stores its own fit's goodness of fit (282 residual degrees of freedom, so 284 points and two coefficients).

In [35]:

rat-perineurium-fit¶

The fit of perineurium thickness against fascicle diameter for 22 rat fascicles has R2 = 0.77.

In [36]:
import numpy.polynomial.polynomial as P
def r2_quad(x, y):
    c = np.polyfit(x, y, 2)
    return 1 - ((y - np.polyval(c, x)) ** 2).sum() / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum(), c
rows_rf = []
for setname, sub in [("(a) all fascicles", PR[PR.species == "rat"]), ("(b) 18 largest", PR[(PR.species == "rat") & PR.largest])]:
    f1 = v.fit_poly1(sub.d, sub.thk)
    f0 = v.fit_poly1(sub.d, sub.thk, intercept=False)
    r2q, cq = r2_quad(sub.d.values, sub.thk.values)
    rows_rf.append(dict(set=setname, n=len(sub), r2_poly1=f1["r2"], p1=f1["p1"], p2=f1["p2"], r2_zero=f0["r2"], slope_zero=f0["p1"], r2_quadratic=r2q))
RF = pd.DataFrame(rows_rf)
print(RF.round(4).to_string())
print("expected n = 22 and R2 = 0.77 +/- 0.077")

                 set   n  r2_poly1      p1      p2  r2_zero  slope_zero  r2_quadratic
0  (a) all fascicles  22    0.7652  0.0129  1.3674   0.5099      0.0197        0.7668
1     (b) 18 largest  18    0.6636  0.0131  1.3119   0.4951      0.0193        0.6686
expected n = 22 and R2 = 0.77 +/- 0.077

Result: reproduced. Every rat fascicle with a thickness, 22 (reading a), fitted by thickness = 0.01292 d + 1.367 um (the code's poly1), gives R2 = 0.765, within 0.77 +/- 0.077. With the 18 largest fascicles R2 = 0.664 (n = 18); through zero R2 = 0.510; a quadratic gives 0.767.

perineurium-species-order¶

For a given fascicle diameter, human fascicles have the thickest perineurium and rat fascicles the thinnest.

In [39]:

hi = min(PR[PR.species == sp].d.max() for sp in fits)

order_a = bool(np.all(pred["human"] > pred["pig"]) and np.all(pred["pig"] > pred["rat"]))

print("(b) fitted thickness at 250 um:", {k: round(x, 2) for k, x in at250.items()}, "| order holds:", at250["human"] > at250["pig"] > at250["rat"])

Result: reproduced. Over the diameters common to all three species (32.0 to 284.1 um) the human fit lies above the pig fit (by at least 7.43 um) and the pig fit above the rat fit (by at least 2.47 um); at 250 um the fits give 19.76, 9.81 and 4.60 um. perineurium-ratio-decreases¶

The ratio of perineurium thickness to fascicle diameter decreases as fascicle diameter increases, particularly in humans and pigs.

In [40]:
for sp, f in fits.items():
    sub = PR[PR.species == sp]
    g = np.linspace(sub.d.min(), sub.d.max(), 100)
    rfit = (f["p1"] * g + f["p2"]) / g
    rho, p = stats.spearmanr(sub.d, sub.ratio)
    print("%s: (a) fitted ratio %.4f at %.0f um to %.4f at %.0f um, decreasing: %s | (b) Spearman rho = %.3f, p = %.2g, n = %d" %
          (sp, rfit[0], g[0], rfit[-1], g[-1], bool(np.all(np.diff(rfit) < 0)), rho, p, len(sub)))

human: (a) fitted ratio 1.5826 at 7 um to 0.0469 at 1061 um, decreasing: True | (b) Spearman rho = -0.919, p = 2.3e-30, n = 73
pig: (a) fitted ratio 0.2649 at 14 um to 0.0368 at 303 um, decreasing: True | (b) Spearman rho = -0.601, p = 2.7e-29, n = 284
rat: (a) fitted ratio 0.0557 at 32 um to 0.0177 at 284 um, decreasing: True | (b) Spearman rho = -0.779, p = 2e-05, n = 22

Result: reproduced. The fitted ratio of thickness to diameter decreases over each species' range (human 1.58 to 0.047, pig 0.265 to 0.037, rat 0.056 to 0.018), and the ratio's Spearman correlation with diameter is negative (human rho = -0.919, pig -0.601, rat -0.779).

perineurium-no-level-difference¶

The relationship between perineurium thickness and fascicle diameter does not differ between cervical and subdiaphragmatic nerves in any of the three species.

In [42]:
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from statsmodels.stats.anova import anova_lm
nld = {}
for sp in ["human", "pig", "rat"]:
    sub = PR[PR.species == sp]
    fc = v.fit_poly1(sub[sub.level == "cervical"].d, sub[sub.level == "cervical"].thk)
    fa = v.fit_poly1(sub[sub.level == "subdiaphragmatic"].d, sub[sub.level == "subdiaphragmatic"].thk)
    overlap = [bool(fc["ci"][i, 0] <= fa["ci"][i, 1] and fa["ci"][i, 0] <= fc["ci"][i, 1]) for i in range(2)]
    m0 = smf.ols("thk ~ d", sub).fit()
    m1 = smf.ols("thk ~ d * C(level)", sub).fit()
    ft = anova_lm(m0, m1)
    nld[sp] = (all(overlap), float(ft["Pr(>F)"].iloc[1]))
    print("%s: cervical n = %d p1 %.4f [%.4f, %.4f] p2 %.3f [%.3f, %.3f] | subdiaphragmatic n = %d p1 %.4f [%.4f, %.4f] p2 %.3f [%.3f, %.3f]" %
          (sp, fc["n"], fc["p1"], *fc["ci"][0], fc["p2"], *fc["ci"][1], fa["n"], fa["p1"], *fa["ci"][0], fa["p2"], *fa["ci"][1]))
    print("    (a) bounds overlap, slope %s, intercept %s | (b) F test of level terms F = %.3f, p = %.3g" %
          (overlap[0], overlap[1], ft["F"].iloc[1], ft["Pr(>F)"].iloc[1]))

human: cervical n = 33 p1 0.0318 [0.0248, 0.0388] p2 10.832 [7.962, 13.702] | subdiaphragmatic n = 40 p1 0.0558 [0.0494, 0.0622] p2 8.609 [7.172, 10.046]
    (a) bounds overlap, slope False, intercept True | (b) F test of level terms F = 19.201, p = 2.35e-07
pig: cervical n = 153 p1 0.0170 [0.0097, 0.0243] p2 5.264 [4.137, 6.392] | subdiaphragmatic n = 131 p1 0.0212 [0.0165, 0.0260] p2 3.159 [2.666, 3.652]
    (a) bounds overlap, slope True, intercept False | (b) F test of level terms F = 21.013, p = 3.14e-09
rat: cervical n = 9 p1 0.0137 [0.0028, 0.0245] p2 1.152 [-1.556, 3.860] | subdiaphragmatic n = 13 p1 0.0149 [0.0037, 0.0261] p2 1.172 [-0.141, 2.484]
    (a) bounds overlap, slope True, intercept True | (b) F test of level terms F = 0.140, p = 0.87

Result: not reproduced (resting on an assumption). Under reading (a), the 95% bounds of the cervical and subdiaphragmatic fits do not overlap for the human slope (0.0318 [0.0248, 0.0388] against 0.0558 [0.0494, 0.0622]) nor for the pig intercept (5.26 [4.14, 6.39] against 3.16 [2.67, 3.65] um); they overlap for both rat coefficients. The F test of the level terms (reading b) agrees: human p = 2.4e-07, pig p = 3.1e-09, rat p = 0.87. The tests are the claims file's, as the paper names none.

sunderland-reanalysis¶

Refitting all 777 fascicles of Sunderland and Bradley (1952) gives a zero-intercept slope of 2.75% of fascicle diameter for perineurium thickness, with R2 = 0.51.

The table is files/code/Sunderland1984.mat of SPARC:65 (fascicle diameter and perineurium thickness, um), with its plotting script Sunderland1984_Plotting.m.

In [43]:

sx, sy = sund["dfasc_um"].astype(float), sund["thk_peri_um"].astype(float)
f0 = v.fit_poly1(sx, sy, intercept=False)
print("n = %d, d %.0f to %.0f um, thickness %.2f to %.2f um" % (len(sx), sx.min(), sx.max(), sy.min(), sy.max()))
print("zero-intercept slope %.4f%% | R2 (about the mean, as MATLAB fit) %.4f | R2 uncentred %.4f" % (100 * f0["p1"], f0["r2"], f0["r2_uncentered"]))
print("ratio of thickness to diameter: mean %.2f%% SD %.2f%%" % (100 * np.mean(sy / sx), 100 * np.std(sy / sx, ddof=1)))

rat-perineurium-near-3-percent¶

Rat perineurium thickness is close to the published 3% of fascicle diameter, slightly thicker for smaller fascicles and thinner for larger ones.

In [44]:
fr_ = fits["rat"]
sub = PR[PR.species == "rat"]
g = np.linspace(sub.d.min(), sub.d.max(), 200)
for slope in [0.03, 0.0275]:
    q = (fr_["p1"] * g + fr_["p2"]) / (slope * g)
    print("reference %.2f%%: fit over reference %.3f at %.1f um to %.3f at %.1f um | within 0.5 to 2: %s | above at smallest: %s, below at largest: %s" %
          (100 * slope, q[0], g[0], q[-1], g[-1], bool(np.all((q > 0.5) & (q < 2))), q[0] > 1, q[-1] < 1))
print("crossing diameter, fit = 3%%: %.1f um" % (fr_["p2"] / (0.03 - fr_["p1"])))

reference 3.00%: fit over reference 1.856 at 32.0 um to 0.591 at 284.1 um | within 0.5 to 2: True | above at smallest: True, below at largest: True
reference 2.75%: fit over reference 2.024 at 32.0 um to 0.645 at 284.1 um | within 0.5 to 2: False | above at smallest: True, below at largest: True
crossing diameter, fit = 3%: 80.1 um

Result: reproduced (resting on an assumption). Against the 3% line, the rat fit over the line runs from 1.856 at 32.0 um to 0.591 at 284.1 um, within a factor of two, above the line for small fascicles and below for large ones (crossing at 80.1 um). Against the 2.75% line the ratio reaches 2.024 at the smallest diameter, just outside a factor of two, so the claim holds under the 3% reading and not quite under the 2.75% one.

human-pig-perineurium-thicker¶

Human and pig vagal perineurium is substantially thicker than the 3% of fascicle diameter found for human somatic nerves, especially for smaller fascicles.

In [45]:
for sp in ["human", "pig", "rat"]:
    sub = PR[PR.species == sp]
    med = sub.d.median()
    exc_s = (sub[sub.d < med].ratio - 0.03).median()
    exc_l = (sub[sub.d >= med].ratio - 0.03).median()
    print("%s: median ratio %.4f | median excess over 0.03, below median diameter %.4f, above %.4f | holds: %s" %
          (sp, sub.ratio.median(), exc_s, exc_l, sub.ratio.median() > 0.03 and exc_s > exc_l))

human: median ratio 0.0948 | median excess over 0.03, below median diameter 0.1061, above 0.0379 | holds: True
pig: median ratio 0.0527 | median excess over 0.03, below median diameter 0.0329, above 0.0160 | holds: True

rat: median ratio 0.0214 | median excess over 0.03, below median diameter -0.0070, above -0.0115 | holds: False

Result: reproduced (resting on an assumption). The median ratio of thickness to diameter is 0.0948 in humans and 0.0527 in pigs, above 0.03, and the median excess over 0.03 is larger below the species' median diameter than above it (human 0.1061 against 0.0379, pig 0.0329 against 0.0160). Rats are below the line (median 0.0214).

pig-if-mt-consistent¶

Pig fascicle diameters from anti-fibronectin IF (14 to 303 um, mean 123, median 123, interquartile range 91 to 155 um) are consistent with those from MT (5 to 399 um, mean 135, median 130, interquartile range 96 to 168 um).

In [46]:
def summ(x):
    x = np.asarray(x)
    return dict(n=len(x), min=x.min(), max=x.max(), mean=x.mean(), median=np.median(x),
                q25=np.percentile(x, 25), q75=np.percentile(x, 75),
                q25_matlab=np.percentile(x, 25, method="hazen"), q75_matlab=np.percentile(x, 75, method="hazen"))
ifx = np.concatenate(if_d)
SU = pd.DataFrame([dict(set="IF non-peanut", **summ(ifx)), dict(set="IF all inner traces", **summ(np.concatenate(if_dall))),
                   dict(set="MT all inner traces", **summ(allpig))])
print(SU.round(1).to_string())
def widen(lo_, hi_):
    return lo_ - 0.1 * lo_, hi_ + 0.1 * hi_
checks = {"IF mean": abs(SU.loc[0, "mean"] - 123) <= 12.3, "IF median": abs(SU.loc[0, "median"] - 123) <= 12.3,
          "MT mean": abs(SU.loc[2, "mean"] - 135) <= 13.5, "MT median": abs(SU.loc[2, "median"] - 130) <= 13}
for name, row, (a_, b_), (c_, d_) in [("IF", 0, (14, 303), (91, 155)), ("MT", 2, (5, 399), (96, 168))]:
    w1, w2 = widen(a_, b_), widen(c_, d_)
    checks[name + " min"] = w1[0] <= SU.loc[row, "min"] <= w1[1]
    checks[name + " max"] = w1[0] <= SU.loc[row, "max"] <= w1[1]
    checks[name + " IQR"] = w2[0] <= SU.loc[row, "q25"] and SU.loc[row, "q75"] <= w2[1]
print(checks)
per_bound = {}
for name, row, bounds in [("IF", 0, dict(min=14, max=303, q25=91, q75=155)), ("MT", 2, dict(min=5, max=399, q25=96, q75=168))]:
    for k, b in bounds.items():
        per_bound[f"{name} {k}"] = bool(abs(SU.loc[row, k] - b) <= 0.1 * b)
print("variant, per-bound reading (each value within 10% of the reported bound):", per_bound)
print("five smallest MT fascicle diameters in SPARC:64's output file (um):", np.round(np.sort(allpig)[:5], 1),
      "| below 10 um:", int((allpig < 10).sum()))

Result: reproduced. IF non-peanut fascicles (284): 14.4 to 302.8 um, mean 123.3, median 123.1, interquartile range 88.1 to 152.5 um; MT fascicles (766): 23.7 to 399.1 um, mean 134.6, median 129.5, interquartile range 95.7 to 167.7 um. Means and medians are within 10%, and the ranges and interquartile ranges lie within the reported ones widened by 10% of each bound, as the criterion says. Read bound by bound, the MT minimum fails: 23.7 um here against the paper's 5 um. SPARC:64's output file has no fascicle below 23.7 um (the five smallest are 23.7 to 31.2 um), so the paper's 5 um fascicle is not in the deposited data.

Result: partially reproduced. Human traces: 60 cervical inner traces with 27 bundles in 10 peanut fascicles and 44 subdiaphragmatic with 4 in 2, as the legend says. Pig IF traces, counted as SPARC:89's code counts them: 210 cervical with 57 bundles in 24 peanut fascicles (the legend says 25) and 179 subdiaphragmatic with 48 in 19, as the legend says. 11 of the 12 counts match. Per sample, the cervical peanut fascicles are 4, 8, 6 and 6 by both counting rules, so the 25th is not found in any sample; the code's own count (Nouterperi_peanut_values) is not saved in PigIFMorphology.mat. The non-peanut sums are 73 (human) and 284 (pig), the fits' counts.

no-age-trend¶

The morphology metrics show no trend with age in any species.

Per species and level, each per-sample metric against the subject's age: nerve diameter, number of fascicles (human and pig), mean fascicle diameter, endoneurium proportion and perineurium proportion (human and rat). Human ages "90+ years" are entered as 99, as the paper's code does (DataExtraction_v3.m). Pig ages take four values (10.5 to 15 weeks). The supplement (Data_Sheet_1.pdf of the Europe PMC supplementary files) is listed and Supplement 6 is printed below: it is one figure of the metrics against age, with no test, so the claims file's tests stand. A Holm correction over the tests is a variant.

            r_, p_ = stats.pearsonr(x, y)
            rs, ps = stats.spearmanr(x, y)

Result: not reproduced (resting on an assumption). Of 26 correlations with age, three have Pearson p < 0.05 (reading a), all in pigs: cervical endoneurium proportion r = -0.72 (p = 0.029), subdiaphragmatic nerve diameter r = 0.75 (p = 0.019) and subdiaphragmatic mean fascicle diameter r = 0.69 (p = 0.039); by Spearman (reading b) one, human subdiaphragmatic mean fascicle diameter (rho = -0.69, p = 0.041). 1.3 would be expected by chance at 0.05. The tests are uncorrected, as the claims file names them; with a Holm correction none is below 0.05 (smallest corrected p 0.499 over all 26 tests, 0.154 within species), which would make the claim reproduced. Supplement 6 is Figure 19, "Nerve morphology metrics versus age", with no test, so the paper's judgement is visual. Whether the criterion should correct for the number of tests is asked of a reader. The pig ages take four values (10.5 to 15 weeks).

rat-carotid-sheath-bundles¶

The rat cervical carotid sheath holds up to six fascicles, of which the largest, taken as the vagus, was segmented.

    im = imagecodecs.jpeg2k_decode(v.read("60", jp), skipres=3)
    peri = v.tif("60", v._prefix("60", int(sub_), int(sam_)) + "PeriMask.tif")
    outer, _ = v.bwboundaries(peri)

        bool(o[:, 0].max() < im.shape[0] and o[:, 1].max() < im.shape[1])))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The derivative folder has the nine cervical micrographs (JPEG 2000), shown above with the trace drawn over each (every trace lies within its image); the legend of Supplementary Figure 16 says these micrographs also show other nerves of the carotid sheath. The dataset holds no trace or label of the other bundles, and the paper does not say how they were identified or counted (its count is from the micrographs of Supplementary Figure 16), so counting them here would be the attempt's own visual judgement, not a measurement. The claim is not tested.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The morphometry repeats the paper's MATLAB code in Python and gives its rat and human values to rounding. The rat "largest fascicle" is the largest by endoneurial area, as the Methods say; the code's first inner trace, which differs in R22-1 and R23-1, is a variant. The mixed models are fitted by REML with unbounded variance components, JMP's default, and tested with Kenward-Roger F tests on the observed REML information, written here and checked on a balanced design; this test gives the paper's F and p for all nine effects it reports (F within 0.4%, with the code's rat values for fascicle diameter), where Kenward-Roger on the expected information gives F up to 5.1% off and degrees of freedom up to twice the paper's. The pig MT and IF values come from the per-fascicle output files of SPARC:64 and SPARC:89, not from their traces (the IF traces are used for counts). Human and pig data come from the sister datasets SPARC:65, SPARC:64 and SPARC:89, and the literature values from Supplement 4. Where the paper names no test (the level comparison of the perineurium fits, the age trends, the literature comparisons), the claims file's tests are used; Supplement 6 shows the age trends as plots only.

What was found about the dataset. The traces of all 18 rat samples are there, and measuring them with the paper's method gives the values of the code folder's output file exactly, and the paper's to rounding (rat nerve diameter 0.2577 and 0.1352 mm against 0.260 and 0.135); the rat subdiaphragmatic fascicle diameter is the paper's (0.121 mm) only under the code's first-trace rule (0.1211 mm, against 0.1291 mm for the largest fascicle). The derivative folder's RatVNMorphology_OutputMetrics.mat is an older output (2020-03-03): it holds all three species (54 samples), its rat values are not those of the traces (cervical nerve diameters up to 8.5 um larger) and its manifest entry describes it as rat metrics. The code folder's output file keeps only 7 of the 22 rat perineurium thicknesses. The readme gives ages 65 to 268 days where subjects.xlsx gives 75 to 268. samples.xlsx does not say that the subdiaphragmatic samples are anterior. In SPARC:65 the NerveMask of C54-3 is inverted (white outside the nerve, filling the frame); it is measured here from its complement, which gives the code folder's 1615 um. The derivative folder holds the rat micrographs (JPEG 2000); the nine cervical ones were opened and drawn with their traces, which lie within each image, and the other bundles of the carotid sheath in them are not traced.
